title: Transport workers: roads, ports and docks
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Bharatiya Parivahan Mazdoor Mahasangh, Private Transport Mazdoor Mahasangh and the Port & Dock federation.
body:
BMS lists several federations in transport: the **Bharatiya Parivahan Mazdoor Mahasangh** (road transport undertakings), the **Bharatiya Private Transport Mazdoor Mahasangh** (workers of private operators) and the **Bharatiya Port & Dock Mazdoor Mahasangh**. The three cover very different workplaces, from a State bus depot to a truck on a highway at night to a quay at a port, but they share one theme: the people who move goods and passengers work long hours, often in difficult conditions, and the safety of everybody else depends on how they are treated.

## Road transport undertakings

State road transport undertakings (SRTUs) run buses in cities, towns and villages, and many people with no other means of travel depend on them. They employ drivers, conductors, mechanics, depot staff, booking clerks and supervisors. Since the workforce is mostly in the organised sector, the questions raised by the Parivahan Mahasangh are the familiar ones of organised labour:

- **Pensions and retirement benefits**, particularly where a corporation has struggled to meet its liabilities;
- **Wage revision**, including timely settlement of arrears;
- **Fleet shortages**, since old buses and unfilled vacancies increase the burden on those in service;
- **The entry of private operators**, through hiring of buses or contracts on routes, and the effect on permanent employment.

These are matters that vary from State to State, because road transport is largely run by State governments and corporations, and the unions therefore negotiate with each of them separately.

## Private transport

Truck, bus and taxi drivers and their helpers, and the staff of private operators, are mostly in the unorganised sector, which means that many have no appointment letter, no fixed wage slip and no social security. Their main concerns are:

- **Duty hours and rest.** Long routes, tight delivery schedules and waiting at loading points push the working day well past what is safe.
- **Overtime** that is either unpaid or paid at the ordinary rate.
- **Insurance and medical care**, because a driver who is injured on the road may have neither.
- **Safe working conditions**, including rest facilities on long routes.

### What the law has said about duty hours

For decades the main law for this sector was the **Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961**. It applied to road transport undertakings with five or more workers, and covered drivers, conductors, cleaners, booking clerks and depot staff. Adults could work eight hours a day and 48 hours a week, with up to ten hours a day allowed on approved long-distance routes. The total span of duty including breaks was capped at twelve hours, a half-hour break was required after five hours of work, nine consecutive hours of rest were required between duties, and overtime was paid at twice the ordinary rate. Operators also had to provide welfare facilities, such as uniforms, medical facilities, a first-aid box in each vehicle and rest rooms at night halts.

This Act has now been subsumed into the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020**, which came into force on 21 November 2025 along with the other Labour Codes. According to a summary of the Code, the coverage threshold rises to ten workers, the eight-hour daily limit is retained, the rest intervals and spread-over are left to the appropriate government (the State, in the case of motor transport undertakings), overtime is still at double rate but now needs the worker's consent, and electronic registration is required. For drivers, the point to watch is what the State rules say about spread-over and rest, because the Code leaves much of that to rules.

## Ports and docks

Ports are national gateways, and a considerable share of the country's trade passes through them. The work of loading, unloading and handling cargo was historically done by a pool of dock workers who were often hired on a casual basis. To bring more regularity into their employment, Parliament passed the **Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act, 1948**, which set up **dock labour boards**. As a document on the dock labour board system explains, these were statutory bodies with equal representation for dock workers and for employers, with the Central Government also represented. They registered dock workers for each port, booked them for work, collected a levy from employers, and paid workers the benefits provided under the scheme, among them minimum guaranteed wages, attendance allowance, pension or provident fund, gratuity and welfare measures.

Over time the system developed difficulties. The same document notes that the workforce often exceeded what regular employment required, which pushed up the levy rate, and some boards adopted voluntary retirement schemes. In 1997 Parliament passed the **Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) (Inapplicability to Major Ports) Act**, which allowed the Central Government to notify that the 1948 Act would cease to apply to a given major port after a settlement between the dock labour board, its workers and the port management. The assets, liabilities and staff of the board then move to the port trust, with employees continuing on terms not less favourable than before. The 1948 Act itself is among the older laws that the Labour Codes were meant to subsume, which is why unions in the sector follow the rules under the OSH Code closely.

The main issues raised by the Port & Dock federation therefore include:

- the **status of dock labour boards** and of the registered workers who remain under them;
- **containerisation and mechanisation**, which reduce the number of people required for a given volume of cargo;
- the effect of **port privatisation** and private terminals on job security;
- **wage settlements** and the timely payment of retirement benefits;
- **safety on the quay**, with heavy equipment and cargo in constant movement.

## The BMS position

BMS says that **duty-hour rules and safety** in transport are matters of public interest. A bus or truck driver who has been at the wheel for far too long is a danger to passengers and other road users alike, and this is why the union argues that the limits on duty hours must be real, monitored and enforced, not just listed in the law. For docks and ports, BMS has stressed that mechanisation and private investment should not mean that existing workers are thrown out without alternatives, that statutory dues must be protected when boards or authorities are restructured, and that workers should be trained for the new equipment. It also asks that unions be consulted when State rules under the Labour Codes are framed, since in many transport matters the rules are made by the State governments.

## What remains to be done

- Registration of private-sector transport workers, so that they can be identified and covered by social security;
- State rules that set clear spread-over and rest periods, with inspections that actually take place;
- Insurance and medical cover for drivers, and rest points on long highways;
- A settled position for dock workers after restructuring, with benefits protected;
- Regular wage revision and pension security in road transport undertakings.

## Transport is life

Whether on a bus, a truck or a ship, the transport worker moves the economy. When he works long hours without rest, the public is at risk as well. For this reason, BMS says that **duty-hour rules and safety** are matters of public interest.
